newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's financial straits temporary - Waigel.
newsitem.headline: Germany's financial straits temporary - Waigel.

text.p: Germany's debt at the end of 1997 is likely to exceed the target for European monetary union, but its current financial straits are temporary, finance minister Theo Waigel said in a paper released on Wednesday.

Tax revenue shortfalls and excess costs for unemployment have totalled tens of billions of marks in the past two years, costs that could not be contained in the short-term by even the most stringent austerity measures, Waigel said.
But the government's reform program for the tax, pension and health care systems will reinforce growth and create jobs, alleviating the budget problems in the medium term, he said.
Privatisation of government assets is a legitimate means of overcoming the temporary hurdles, to avoid burdening future budgets with additional debt service costs, he said.

Germany has confronted enormous financial challenges since reunification in 1990, absorbing 450 billion marks of communist-era east German debt and transferring an additional 130 to 140 billion marks annually to put the new states back on their feet, Waigel said.
An additional 160 billion marks went in aid and loans for former Soviet states and east European neighbours.

Without such extraordinary expenditures, Germany's would have a budget surplus of two percent of gross domestic product, instead of the deficit of three percent of GDP projected for this year, the level needed to qualify for European monetary union, he said.
Germany's outstanding debt will be about 60.5 percent of GDP at the end of this year, just above the 60 percent target for EMU, he said.
About 570 billion marks of the total 2.22 trillion marks in debt was due to such extraordinary factors, he said.

The end of some spending programmes such as coal subsidies, the government's move to Berlin and lower payouts for victims of World War Two will improve the financial picture after the turn of the century, he said.
The government's share of the overall economy will edge down to 49.5 percent of GDP this year and 48.5 percent next year from over 50 percent this year.
Tax levels this year will fall below the pre-unification levels, he said.
